ds-stack-permutation.trap: "2, 4, 3, 1" looks impossible because 1 comes out last, but push 1, push 2, pop 2, push 3, push 4, pop 4, pop 3, pop 1 produces it.

ds-queue-two-stacks.shortcut: Count total work, not the worst call: no element is pushed or popped more than twice, so any sequence of n operations costs O(n) in all, which is O(1) per operation.
ds-queue-two-stacks.trap: O(n) prices the single worst dequeue, the one that empties A into B, instead of averaging over the sequence as amortised cost requires.

ds-circular-queue-count.shortcut: rear sits one slot behind front, (3 + 1) mod 8 = 4, which is the definition of full in the one-empty-slot scheme: capacity 8 − 1 = 7.
ds-circular-queue-count.trap: 1 takes the gap front − rear = 4 − 3 without adding n, measuring the empty stretch instead of the occupied one.

ds-level-order-structure.shortcut: Nodes must leave in the order they were discovered, level by level, which is first in, first out; a heap orders by key and a hash table has no order, so a queue.
ds-level-order-structure.trap: "A stack" is the usual tool for tree traversals through recursion, but last in, first out dives deep and produces a depth-first order.

ds-singly-list-o1-operation.shortcut: With only a head pointer, anything that needs the last node or a search walks n links; only the front needs no traversal.
ds-singly-list-o1-operation.trap: "Inserting a node at the end" is O(1) only when a tail pointer is kept, and this list has just the head.

ds-dll-insert-pointers.shortcut: Count the arrows touching the new node: two leaving it (prev and next) and two entering it (the predecessor's next and the successor's prev), which makes 4.
ds-dll-insert-pointers.trap: 2 carries over the singly linked count, forgetting that the new node's prev and the successor's prev must also be set.

ds-circular-list-tail-pointer.shortcut: tail.next is the head, so a tail pointer reaches both ends in one hop; front and end insertion are the same splice, differing only in whether tail moves.
ds-circular-list-tail-pointer.trap: "At the end only" reasons as for a plain tail pointer and forgets that circularity hands over the head for free.

ds-loop-detection.shortcut: O(1) space rules out anything that stores nodes, the hash set and the sorted addresses, and Kadane's algorithm solves maximum subarray, which leaves the two-pointer method.
ds-loop-detection.trap: "Recording every visited node in a hash set" does detect a loop and is the usual first idea, but it needs O(n) space.

ds-max-nodes-height.shortcut: Height 5 counted in edges means 6 full levels, 2⁶ − 1 = 63; a count of the form 2ᵏ − 1 is always odd, which rules out 32 and 64.
ds-max-nodes-height.trap: 31 is 2⁵ − 1, the formula for height counted in nodes; with a single node at height 0 the tree has one more level.

ds-full-binary-tree-leaves.shortcut: Count edges: 10 internal nodes with 2 children each give 20 edges, so 21 nodes in all, and 21 − 10 = 11 are leaves.
ds-full-binary-tree-leaves.trap: 20 counts two leaves per internal node, forgetting that most of those children are themselves internal nodes.

ds-postorder-from-two-traversals.shortcut: Each subtree ends with its own root: the left subtree rooted at B reads D E B, the right rooted at C with F on its right reads F C, then A.
ds-postorder-from-two-traversals.trap: "D B E F C A" copies the left subtree in inorder (D B E) instead of postorder, putting B before its right child E.

ds-bst-inorder-sorted.shortcut: In a BST left < node < right, so visiting left, node, right yields increasing keys, and that is exactly inorder.
ds-bst-inorder-sorted.trap: "Preorder" tempts as the traversal usually listed first and the one that rebuilds a BST, but it starts at the root, which is rarely the smallest key.

ds-bst-search-worst.shortcut: Worst case means worst shape: keys inserted in sorted order make a chain of height n − 1, so a search can take O(n).
ds-bst-search-worst.trap: "O(log n)" is the balanced or average case, guaranteed only by self-balancing trees such as AVL, not by a plain BST.

ds-bst-delete-two-children.shortcut: The inorder successor is the next larger key: in 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80 the key after 50 is 60.
ds-bst-delete-two-children.trap: 40 is the inorder predecessor, the largest key in the left subtree; it is a valid replacement in general, but not the successor asked for.

ds-bst-preorder-to-postorder.shortcut: Postorder puts each subtree's root after its children: 30 must follow 20 and 40, and 70 must come just before the final 50, and only one option has both.
ds-bst-preorder-to-postorder.trap: "20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80" is the sorted order, which is the inorder traversal of any BST, not the postorder.

ds-avl-min-nodes.shortcut: The minimum is N(h) = F(h + 3) − 1 with Fibonacci 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, so N(4) = F(7) − 1 = 13 − 1 = 12.
ds-avl-min-nodes.trap: 7 is N(3), the answer one level down, which is what counting height in nodes rather than edges produces.

ds-min-heap-insert.shortcut: 5 sifts up along its own path only, index 5 → 2 → 0, so 20, 30 and 40 never move, and the displaced 15 and 10 each drop one level.
ds-min-heap-insert.trap: "5, 20, 15, 30, 40, 10" swaps the new key straight with the root, skipping its parent 15 on the way up.

ds-valid-max-heap.shortcut: Check the last parent first: in six elements index 2 has one child, index 5, and 7 < 10 kills [9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 10]; the root kills [8, 9, …] and 5 < 6 kills [10, 5, 9, 2, 6, 3].
ds-valid-max-heap.trap: "[9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 10]" is almost descending and looks heap-like, but 10 sits at index 5 as a child of 7.

ds-heap-extract-max.shortcut: After 50 goes, the new root must be the larger child 40, which rules out 35 at the top; 35 then lands at index 2, a leaf, and 30, 10 and 20 never move.
ds-heap-extract-max.trap: "35, 30, 40, 10, 20" moves the last leaf to the root and stops, skipping the sift-down against the larger child 40.

ds-quicksort-worst-case.shortcut: Sorted input with a first-element pivot is quicksort's textbook worst case: every split is 0 against n − 1, so the recursion is n deep with linear work per level.
ds-quicksort-worst-case.trap: "O(n log n)" is quicksort's average case, quoted without checking that this pivot rule makes every partition lopsided.

ds-lomuto-partition.shortcut: Lomuto keeps the small keys in the order it meets them, 2, 1, 3, which rules out two options; the final pivot swap sends the large key at index 3, 6, to the last slot, which rules out the option ending in 7.
ds-lomuto-partition.trap: "1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 5, 7, 6" sorts the left part, as though partitioning ordered it; 2 is met before 1 and stays in front.

ds-unstable-sort.shortcut: Instability comes from long-distance swaps; of these four only quicksort's partition makes them, while the other three never move one equal key past another.
ds-unstable-sort.trap: "Merge sort" splits and recombines, so it looks as if it could scramble equal keys, but taking from the left run on a tie keeps it stable.

ds-bubble-sort-swaps.shortcut: On a reversed array every comparison finds the larger element in front, so the passes swap 4, 3, 2 and 1 times: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10.
ds-bubble-sort-swaps.trap: 4 counts only the swaps in the first pass, which carries 5 to the end; three more passes are still needed.

ds-insertion-sort-best.shortcut: Best case is stated for a general n, which rules out the single-element O(1); on sorted input each element costs one failed comparison, so O(n).
ds-insertion-sort-best.trap: "O(1) on a single-element array" is the fastest possible run, but best case is defined for inputs of arbitrary size n.

ds-merge-sort-space.shortcut: Heapsort, insertion sort and selection sort all work in place with swaps; only merging needs a scratch buffer as long as the runs, O(n).
ds-merge-sort-space.trap: "Heapsort" shares merge sort's O(n log n) guarantee, so it is assumed to share the memory cost, but it sorts in place.

ds-binary-search-comparisons.shortcut: Halve until nothing is left: 1000 → 500 → 250 → 125 → 62 → 31 → 15 → 7 → 3 → 1 is ten probes.
ds-binary-search-comparisons.trap: 9 is ⌊log₂ 1000⌋ without the +1; 2⁹ = 512 positions are too few to cover 1000.

ds-min-max-comparisons.shortcut: Each of the 99 non-maxima must lose once and each of the 99 non-minima must win once, 198 verdicts; only the 50 opening pairings of untouched elements deliver two verdicts at once, so 198 − 50 = 148.
ds-min-max-comparisons.trap: 198 runs two separate scans of 99 comparisons each, never letting one comparison serve both the minimum and the maximum.

ds-linear-probing-index.shortcut: All three keys hash to 2, so they fill consecutive slots from 2 in insertion order, and the third lands at 2 + 2 = 4.
ds-linear-probing-index.trap: 3 probes only one step past the home slot, forgetting that 22 already took index 3.

ds-primary-clustering.shortcut: Primary clustering needs a fixed step of 1 so that runs merge; quadratic probing and double hashing vary the step, and chaining keeps keys outside the table.
ds-primary-clustering.trap: "Quadratic probing" suffers secondary clustering, and the similar name makes it tempting, but it cures the primary kind.

ds-complete-graph-edges.shortcut: Each of the 12 vertices has degree 11, and each edge is counted from both ends: 12 × 11 ÷ 2 = 66.
ds-complete-graph-edges.trap: 132 is 12 × 11 without halving, which counts each undirected edge twice, as if the graph were directed.

ds-adjacency-list-space.shortcut: One header per vertex plus one node per edge end: isolated vertices still need their headers and dense graphs still need their nodes, so neither term can be dropped.
ds-adjacency-list-space.trap: "O(E)" counts only the list nodes and forgets the V headers, which dominate when the graph has few edges.

ds-dfs-order.shortcut: A → B → D → E is forced; at E the alphabetical rule picks C before F, and C is a dead end, so F comes last.
ds-dfs-order.trap: "A, B, C, D, E, F" is the breadth-first order, visiting A's neighbours B and C before going deeper.

ds-bfs-shortest-path.shortcut: F's only neighbour is E, and E is two hops from A through C, so the distance to F is 2 + 1 = 3.
ds-bfs-shortest-path.trap: 4 follows the depth-first route A → B → D → E → F instead of the shorter path through C.

ds-topological-sort-condition.shortcut: A topological order exists exactly for DAGs: a directed cycle would force a vertex to come before itself, and connectivity plays no part.
ds-topological-sort-condition.trap: "is strongly connected" sounds rigorous, but a strongly connected graph with two or more vertices always contains a cycle, so it rules an order out.

ds-row-major-address.shortcut: Each row is 20 × 4 = 80 bytes: three whole rows are 240 bytes and five elements add 20, so 1000 + 260 = 1260.
ds-row-major-address.trap: 1320 is 1000 + 4 × 80, which counts row 3 itself as a whole row and ignores the column offset; only rows 0 to 2 precede it.

ds-fib-recursive-calls.shortcut: Every non-base call has exactly two children, so calls = 2 × leaves − 1; the leaves are the fib(1) and fib(0) calls, fib(6) = 8 of them, giving 15.
ds-fib-recursive-calls.trap: 8 counts only the base-case calls at the leaves of the call tree and forgets the 7 internal calls that spawned them.

ds-tower-of-hanoi-moves.shortcut: 2⁶ − 1 = 63; the count 2M + 1 is always odd, which rules out 36 and 64 on sight.
ds-tower-of-hanoi-moves.trap: 64 is 2⁶ without the −1, from misremembering the formula 2ⁿ − 1.

cs-fcfs-avg-waiting.shortcut: Weight each burst by how many processes queue behind it: 24 × 2 + 3 × 1 + 3 × 0 = 51, and 51 ÷ 3 = 17.
cs-fcfs-avg-waiting.trap: 27 is the average completion time, (24 + 27 + 30) ÷ 3, which is turnaround rather than waiting time.

cs-sjf-avg-waiting.shortcut: Sort the bursts to 3, 6, 7, 8; each delays every job after it, so the total wait is 3 × 3 + 6 × 2 + 7 × 1 = 28, and 28 ÷ 4 = 7.
cs-sjf-avg-waiting.trap: 7.75 runs P1 first because it is listed first and only then goes shortest-first, giving waits 0, 6, 9 and 16, which total 31.

cs-round-robin-waiting.shortcut: P2 and P3 finish in their first turn, so they wait 4 and 7; P1 waits only between its first slice and its return, 10 − 4 = 6. The total 17 ÷ 3 = 5.67.
cs-round-robin-waiting.trap: 7.00 takes P1's wait as 10, the time it resumes, without subtracting the 4 units it had already run: (10 + 4 + 7) ÷ 3 = 7.

cs-srtf-avg-waiting.shortcut: Total waiting = sum of completions − sum of arrivals − sum of bursts = (5 + 10 + 17 + 26) − 6 − 26 = 26, so the average is 6.50.
cs-srtf-avg-waiting.trap: 7.75 runs the jobs without preemption: P1 keeps the CPU to 8, then P2, P4 and P3 follow, giving waits 0, 7, 9 and 15, which total 31.

cs-deadlock-not-a-condition.shortcut: Coffman's four are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait; priority inversion is a scheduling problem outside that list.
cs-deadlock-not-a-condition.trap: "Mutual exclusion" sounds like a safeguard rather than a cause, so candidates strike it out, but deadlock is impossible on shareable resources, which makes it the first of the four.

cs-deadlock-resource-ordering.shortcut: A cycle needs someone holding a higher number while requesting a lower one; increasing-order requests make every wait point upwards, so no cycle can close.
cs-deadlock-resource-ordering.trap: "Hold and wait" tempts because the rule restricts requests, but processes still hold lower-numbered resources while waiting for higher ones.

cs-min-resources-deadlock-free.shortcut: 8 units is the largest pool that can still deadlock, every process stuck at 2 of its 3; one more unit always lets someone finish, so 9.
cs-min-resources-deadlock-free.trap: 8 stops at the deadlocked allocation of 2 units each and forgets the extra unit that breaks the stalemate.

cs-fifo-page-faults.shortcut: Count the hits instead: only the 1 and 2 straight after the 5, and the final 5, find their page resident, so 12 − 3 = 9 faults.
cs-fifo-page-faults.trap: 10 is what LRU gives on this string with three frames, and FIFO with four; mixing up the policy or remembering Belady's larger figure lands on it.

cs-lru-page-faults.shortcut: Only the two re-references to 0 hit, because 0 is always recent when it returns, so 8 − 2 = 6 faults.
cs-lru-page-faults.trap: 7 is the FIFO count: evicting the oldest-loaded page throws 0 out at the reference to 3, so the next 0 faults as well.

cs-belady-anomaly.shortcut: OPT is optimal for every frame count, so an extra frame cannot hurt it, and LRU shares its nesting property; that rules out three options at once.
cs-belady-anomaly.trap: "LRU" tempts as the other everyday policy, but LRU is a stack algorithm, so more frames can never cause more faults.

cs-page-table-entries.trap: "2^12 (4 K)" confuses the 12 offset bits of a 4 KB page with the page-number bits; 12 bits index bytes inside a page, not pages.

cs-tlb-effective-access.shortcut: Every access pays 20 + 100 ns and only the misses pay a second 100: 120 + 0.2 × 100 = 140 ns.
cs-tlb-effective-access.trap: "120 ns" is the cost of a hit alone, ignoring the 20% of accesses that must also read the page table.

cs-internal-fragmentation.shortcut: A 10 KB process in 4 KB pages takes 3 pages, 12 KB, and wastes 2 KB inside its last page; waste inside an allocation is internal fragmentation.
cs-internal-fragmentation.trap: "Segmentation" is famous for fragmentation, but its waste is external: holes between variable-sized segments, not inside them.

cs-thread-private-stack.shortcut: Two threads can be inside different functions at once, so each needs its own return addresses and program counter, the stack and registers; the rest is process-wide.
cs-thread-private-stack.trap: "The global data section" feels per-thread because each thread can change globals, but they are shared, which is exactly why races happen.

cs-counting-semaphore-value.trap: 4 is 10 − 6, applying the waits and forgetting the four signals that add units back.

cs-relation-2nf-not-3nf.shortcut: Look for a non-key attribute determining another non-key attribute: B → C is one, so 3NF fails; 2NF can fail only through part of a composite key, and A stands alone.
cs-relation-2nf-not-3nf.trap: "3NF but not BCNF" treats B → C as only a BCNF violation, but 3NF's exemption needs a prime attribute on the right, and C is not prime.

cs-3nf-not-bcnf.shortcut: AB → C with C → B is the textbook gap: C is not a superkey, so BCNF fails, but B is prime, so 3NF holds.
cs-3nf-not-bcnf.trap: "2NF but not 3NF" reads C → B as a transitive dependency, missing that B belongs to the candidate key AB and so is exempt.

cs-candidate-key-count.shortcut: B cannot be derived, so pair it with each other attribute and take closures: AB, BC and BD each reach all of A, B, C, D, while B alone reaches nothing, giving 3.
cs-candidate-key-count.trap: 1 stops at AB, the key visible on a left-hand side, without testing BC and BD.

cs-sql-having-average.shortcut: Only Sales can be borderline: (30000 + 50000) ÷ 2 = 40000 exactly, which fails the strict > 40000, while HR (50000) and IT (45000) pass.
cs-sql-having-average.trap: "Sales, HR and IT" treats > as >=, keeping Sales although its average equals 40000 exactly.

cs-sql-count-null.shortcut: COUNT(column) = rows − NULLs in that column = 5 − 2 = 3, beside COUNT(*) = 5.
cs-sql-count-null.trap: "5 and 5" assumes COUNT(manager_id) counts every row, NULL included.

cs-left-outer-join-rows.shortcut: Rows = the sum over students of max(matches, 1): Asha 2, Ravi 1 padded with NULLs, Meena 1, which makes 4.
cs-left-outer-join-rows.trap: 3 assumes a left join returns exactly one row per left-table row, but Asha matches two marks and appears twice.

cs-natural-join-max-tuples.shortcut: No join can exceed the cross product, and it is reached when every tuple shares a single B value: 200 × 100 = 20000.
cs-natural-join-max-tuples.trap: 200 assumes each R tuple matches at most one S tuple, which holds only if B is a key of S.

cs-sql-clause-order.shortcut: Eliminate the rules SQL does not have: WHERE can filter unindexed columns, letter case is not what blocks the alias, and both clauses run on the server, which leaves evaluation order.
cs-sql-clause-order.trap: "ORDER BY runs on the client and WHERE runs on the server" sounds plausible because sorting feels like presentation, but the database engine runs both.

cs-truncate-vs-delete.shortcut: DROP removes the table itself and UPDATE removes nothing; of the two that empty a table, DELETE is DML, so TRUNCATE.
cs-truncate-vs-delete.trap: "DELETE" does remove every row when given no WHERE and keeps the table, but it is DML, not DDL.

cs-acid-durability.shortcut: Atomicity and isolation govern work still in progress and consistency governs valid states; only durability speaks about changes after the commit, which is when the power fails here.
cs-acid-durability.trap: "Atomicity" is linked with crash recovery, but it concerns undoing uncommitted work as all or nothing, not keeping committed work.

cs-isolation-level-dirty-read.shortcut: The name says it: Read Committed reads only committed data, so no dirty reads, but holds no read locks to the end, so a re-read can change.
cs-isolation-level-dirty-read.trap: "Repeatable Read" also prevents dirty reads, but it prevents non-repeatable reads too, which the question says must still be allowed.

cs-clustered-index.shortcut: Eliminate: the primary key is the usual clustered index, its leaves hold the rows, and one per column would need several physical row orders at once, which leaves at most one per table.
cs-clustered-index.trap: "A clustered index stores only pointers and never the rows themselves" describes a non-clustered index; a clustered index's leaves are the rows.

cs-primary-key-vs-unique.shortcut: PRIMARY KEY = UNIQUE + NOT NULL, and only one option matches that equation.
cs-primary-key-vs-unique.trap: "Neither allows NULL, and a table may have only one of each" tempts because both reject duplicates, but UNIQUE accepts NULL and a table may carry several UNIQUE constraints.

cs-router-layer.shortcut: Forwarding between networks by IP address is routing, and IP is the layer 3 protocol; forwarding by MAC address would make it a switch at layer 2.
cs-router-layer.trap: "Data link layer" tempts because a router's interfaces handle frames and MAC addresses, but its forwarding decision uses the IP address, which is layer 3.

cs-presentation-layer.shortcut: Encryption, compression and encoding change how data is represented, not where it goes, which is the job of layer 6, presentation.
cs-presentation-layer.trap: "Application layer" is right for TCP/IP, where these duties fold into the application, but the question asks about the OSI model.

cs-tcp-not-a-feature.shortcut: 8 bytes is UDP's header, four 2-byte fields; TCP's minimum is 20, and the other three statements are TCP's defining features.
cs-tcp-not-a-feature.trap: "It delivers bytes to the application in order" tempts because IP packets can arrive out of order, but TCP reorders them by sequence number.

cs-three-way-handshake.shortcut: Nothing can be acknowledged before it is sent, so SYN must come first and a bare ACK last, and only SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK fits.
cs-three-way-handshake.trap: "SYN, ACK, SYN-ACK" starts correctly, but the server does not acknowledge first and send its own SYN separately; one SYN-ACK does both.

cs-dns-port.shortcut: Three of the options are file or mail transfer ports (20 FTP data, 25 SMTP, 110 POP3), so the odd one out, 53, is DNS.
cs-dns-port.trap: 25 tempts because DNS MX lookups are bound up with mail delivery, but 25 is SMTP itself.

cs-dns-a-record.shortcut: A stands for address (IPv4) and AAAA for the four-times-longer IPv6 address; CNAME aliases, MX names mail servers and NS names name servers.
cs-dns-a-record.trap: "CNAME" also starts from a host name, but it maps that name to another name, never to an IP address.

cs-subnet-usable-hosts.shortcut: A /26 is a quarter of a /24's 256 addresses, 64, and removing the network and broadcast addresses leaves 62.
cs-subnet-usable-hosts.trap: 64 counts all 2⁶ addresses and forgets that the all-zeros and all-ones host values are reserved.

cs-broadcast-address.shortcut: A broadcast address has all host bits set, so it must be odd, which rules out .64; .63 belongs to the block before 75, and .255 would need a /24 mask.
cs-broadcast-address.trap: "192.168.10.255" applies the default /24 broadcast and ignores the .192 mask that cuts the octet into blocks of 64.

cs-http-403.shortcut: "Understood but refused, and retrying will not help" rules out a redirect (301), a missing resource (404) and 401, whose whole purpose is to invite a retry with credentials.
cs-http-403.trap: "401 Unauthorized" matches the wording "refuses to authorise", but 401 really means unauthenticated and invites a retry with credentials.

cs-switch-domains.shortcut: A switch gives each port its own collision domain (24) and floods broadcasts everywhere, so only a router or VLAN would split the single broadcast domain.
cs-switch-domains.trap: "1 collision domain and 1 broadcast domain" is the answer for a hub, which shares one medium among all its ports.

cs-tcp-flow-control.shortcut: Flow control protects the receiver, so the receiver must set the limit, and only the advertised-window option involves the receiver at all.
cs-tcp-flow-control.trap: "The slow-start congestion window" also throttles the sender, but it protects the network (congestion control), not the receiver.

cs-go-back-n-window.shortcut: A memory hook: the largest Go-Back-N window equals the largest sequence number, 2⁴ − 1 = 15.
cs-go-back-n-window.trap: 16 uses all 2⁴ sequence numbers, which lets a fully retransmitted window be mistaken for a fresh one.
